articles.sourceTitle: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
articles.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights
articles.text:
TL;DR
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

Read
Which game was this neural network trained on?

Astra reads the 17,253 weights, with no tools
Breakout 99% confident

Fix
A trained policy never gets the car over the strip.

Astra edits 3.5% of the weights, in one shot
100% success, up from 0%

Improve
Make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math.

7.9%base
7.9%Astra’s edit

Astra edits the weights in a Python kernel, with no training
48.1% on MATH-500, up from 7.9%

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.
Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

Weight-Space Programming
For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses  and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .
We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.
In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.
In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.
In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic.
LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too.
LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go.

Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights?

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

Experiment 1Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights?

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

Setup

Games: our own grid versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway, all on the same 10×10 grid with the same five actions
Network: MLP 500 → 32 → 32 → 5, tanh (17,253 weights), the same for every game
Input: the 10×10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame
Output: 5 action logits: no-op, up, down, left, right
Training: PPO, 1 billion steps, the same settings for every game, the best of 3 seeds per game
Astra gets: all the weights as text, and the grid and actions described without any game named

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Experiment 2Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate?

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

Setup

Models: three diffusion models (DDPM) of 12×12 grayscale images, one each for filled circles, squares and triangles
Network: MLP 160 → 64 → 64 → 144, ReLU (23,824 weights)
Input: a noisy image (144 pixels) and the diffusion step (16 numbers)
Output: the clean image (144 pixels)
Training: Adam, 40,000 steps, batch 512
Astra gets: all the weights as text, with no shape named, and is told not to compute any forward pass

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes.  This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.
Experiment 3Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone?

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

Figure 1: The copying heads Astra read from the weights match the measured ones in all three models.

Setup

Models: character-level transformers, 4 layers × 6 heads, width 384 (7.16 million weights), 28 characters: a–z, space and newline
Training: 1 billion characters each, of Python code, Japanese literature in romaji (Aozora Bunko), or English Wikipedia
Astra gets: the weights of the four transformer blocks only, with no input layer, no output layer and no labels on the 384 dimensions, and Python to analyze them, up to 100 runs
Not allowed: running the network or any of its layers on any input, real, random or made up, and search. We checked every run
Asked: which of the three texts the network was trained on, and what each head does
Truth: each head measured by running the network on a random string repeated twice. Copying heads score 0.22 to 0.55, every other head at most 0.02. Astra never sees this

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.

Can an LLM write neural network weights?

So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.

Experiment 4Can Astra fix a failing network by editing its weights?

We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate lon

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic's internal AI use, at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay
articles.title: Anthropic's Internal AI Usage Now Exceeds Employee Compensation
articles.text:
Anthropic's internal AI use, valued at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images

This story is available exclusively to Business Insider
subscribers. Become an Insider
and start reading now.
Have an account? .

Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees.The company revealed this in its IPO filing. In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards. By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January.There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices.Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry.In March, I wrote about a new trend: Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards.Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount.For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption.Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com

Read next

Alistair Barr is the driving force behind Business Insider's AI Insider franchise, including the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up here. Before that, he was Business Insider's Global Tech Editor and the Big Tech team leader at Bloomberg, following a reporting career at The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Reuters, and MarketWatch. Alistair covers all things Big Tech, along with startups and venture capital. He writes analysis and columns about topics including AI, cloud computing, data centers, semiconductors, online search, e-commerce, EVs, robotics, and autonomous vehicles.

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic reports $17B in Q3 revenue, commitments of $895B in revised S-1
articles.title: Anthropic releases amended IPO prospectus with Q3 financials
articles.text:
Tech

Anthropic reports $17 billion in Q3 revenue, purchase commitments of $895.4 billion in revised S-1

Published Mon, Nov 2 20269:32 AM ESTUpdated 4 Hours Ago

Key Points

Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.
Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, but the initial filing only included the company's financials through the first half of the year.

Anthropic

reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.
The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.

Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.
During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.
The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.

Read more CNBC Anthropic news

As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft

, Alphabet

and Amazon

last week added fuel to those concerns.
The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.

In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.
"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.
The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI

, now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut.
Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.
"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.
WATCH: Anthropic releases amended IPO prospectus with third-quarter financials

articles.sourceTitle: Jobless tech workers are being left out of San Francisco's AI boom
AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System
articles.title: AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System.
articles.text: When people say AI has transformed software development, I want to know which part they mean. Producing an implementation? Exploring a design? Deciding whether a system solves the right problem?Those activities are connected, but automating one does not settle the others. My argument is that agents can take on more implementation work, and assist with analysis, design, and testing, while engineers remain responsible for deciding what to build and what evidence is sufficient to accept it.That changes the work. It does not make the responsibilities disappear.I am wary of describing this as replacing the person who churns out code. It reduces developers to typing, understates what agents can assist with, and turns task automation into a claim about jobs. Claims about workforce replacement require evidence beyond an impressive demonstration.The practical question interests me more: how do we use these tools while keeping our decisions visible and our feedback useful?Give decisions somewhere to liveA conversation is convenient for exploring options. It is a fragile place to keep the only record of an architectural decision.Model context is bounded. A long session may be summarized, compacted, or resumed with selected information. The summary can preserve the conclusion and lose the condition that made it reasonable. “Use a local cache” is different from “use a local cache because this screen must remain usable without connectivity.”Anthropic's account of long-running agents describes continuity problems across context windows and an approach using incremental work and persistent progress artifacts. It also reports that compaction can leave unclear instructions. This is a vendor engineering report about a particular setup, rather than a universal comparison of development workflows.My preference is to give durable decisions a small, reviewable home. A PROJECT_GUIDE.md might contain:The product's purpose and current scope, including explicit exclusions.The important system boundaries and the reasons behind architectural choices.Quality expectations and the commands used to check them.Links to deeper decisions when those decisions need more space.The filename has no special power. An agent will not necessarily load it automatically. I would connect it through the tool's supported project instructions or explicitly include it in the task, then check the agent's interpretation.For each increment, I would supply the relevant files and ask for a brief account of the intended change, constraints, and acceptance cases. A paraphrase is an early opportunity to catch misunderstanding; the implementation still has to demonstrate compliance.Simon Willison's June 2025 discussion of context engineering helps frame the problem of choosing information for the next model step. My narrower recommendation is to make that selection deliberate and inspect its consequences.Markdown alone guarantees neither retrieval nor obedience. Sending every document on every task can increase context and cost. Selective retrieval may reduce input, but maintaining documents, retrieving them, and correcting mistakes also consume resources. Any claim of savings needs a measurement of the complete task.Specify the next behaviorConsider a hypothetical mobile search screen. This is an illustration, not a report from a completed project.The story could be: “As a user, I want to search saved items so that I can find an item without scrolling through the entire collection.” For the first increment, the scope is local search over existing items. Remote search and changes to persistence are excluded.Before implementation, I would make these acceptance cases explicit:A matching query displays the expected items.A query with no matches displays an empty result state.Clearing the query restores the complete collection.If filtering is asynchronous, an older result cannot overwrite a newer query's results.These cases expose a technical question: does filtering need asynchronous work at all? The agent can help assess that decision. We should resolve it against the expected data size and responsiveness requirements, rather than introducing concurrency because a template expects it.For this example, I might choose unidirectional data flow, explicit UI states, and a separation between filtering logic and rendering. That makes state transitions easier to inspect. Another system may justify a different structure; this is an engineering choice with a purpose.The project guide should preserve that purpose. Feature-level notes should explain the behavior and any new decision. They do not need to reproduce the entire architecture.After the increment, I would inspect the diff, run the relevant checks, and exercise the screen. If the agent rewrote persistence despite the scope restriction, passing tests would not make that expansion acceptable. If the empty state looks correct but the search matches the wrong field, a screenshot would not establish correctness either.Make generation answer to verificationAgent output is probabilistic. Acceptance should depend on evidence that we can inspect and, where practical, reproduce.A local verification command can run formatting checks, static analysis, compilation, and focused tests. These checks answer different questions. A formatter checks conventions; a compiler checks language and type rules; tests evaluate selected behavior under selected conditions. None establishes that we chose the right product behavior.Controlled verification also needs controlled inputs. Tool versions, fixtures, and execution conditions matter. Tests involving timing, devices, networks, or external services may be flaky. Calling a test suite deterministic does not make it so.Even a perfectly repeatable check can verify the wrong thing. A search test might assert that some result appears without checking which result it is. A generated test can faithfully encode the same misunderstanding as the generated implementation. I would review the assertion against the acceptance case and use deliberately chosen examples, including a failure case.Running the app adds another kind of evidence: whether the behavior makes sense through the actual interface. When performance matters, define the measurement before declaring success—device, dataset, scenario, and threshold. A quick impression of responsiveness is useful feedback, but it is not a latency result.Hooks can make local checks convenient and catch mistakes earlier. Their coverage depends on what triggers them and whether they can be bypassed. Where a team requires enforcement, server-side checks and repository protections need their own configuration. A local hook is not equivalent to an enforced remote policy.The engineer still decides whether the evidence supports acceptance, revision, or rejection. An agent can help gather that evidence; it cannot make an incomplete test suite complete by announcing success.Documentation has to earn its maintenanceI become skeptical when a small change requires a long chain of generated documents before anyone can see working behavior. Each document becomes something to review, reconcile, and keep current. Producing text cheaply does not make understanding it cheap.That is a criticism of proportionality and feedback cadence. Spec-driven development has multiple meanings. Birgitta Böckeler's 2025 examination of Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl distinguishes approaches that write specifications first, retain them during maintenance, or treat them as the primary source. Those differences matter when discussing costs and control.François Zaninotto's critique of document-heavy workflows raises concerns about review overhead and instruction following through reported examples. Those cases are useful prompts for investigation. They do not establish that specifications generally cause worse outcomes.An incremental specification can support rapid feedback. Agile does not mean avoiding documentation: its principles emphasize frequent working software, technical excellence, and adaptation. A short acceptance case can serve those aims; so can a detailed design when the risk warrants it.Stronger specifications can be valuable for safety constraints, regulated work, public interfaces, migration compatibility, and coordination across teams. In those settings, a concise guide is an entry point to the necessary detail. It cannot replace that detail.My test for a document is practical: what decision, implementation, or verification does it support, and who will maintain it? I would keep the explanation of a compatibility constraint even if it takes several pages. I would remove repeated prose that neither changes a decision nor helps someone evaluate the work.Matt Pocock's collection of engineering skills offers another example of packaging guidance into adaptable, composable pieces. I find that direction useful. Its stated design goals are not evidence that a collection of skills outperforms another workflow.Keep the acceptance decision explicitA small increment can still contain a bad assumption. Its advantage is that it gives us an earlier, more bounded opportunity to discover one.The loop I would advocate is straightforward: define the next behavior, supply the context it needs, check the interpretation, inspect the change, collect evidence, and decide whether to accept it. Update durable guidance when a decision changes. If review becomes unmanageable, reduce the increment or improve the checks before asking the agent to produce more.This approach has limits. It depends on the engineer's understanding, the quality of the evidence, and the cost of keeping guidance current. This article presents a working position, not a controlled study or a demonstrated productivity gain. Establishing such a gain would require comparable tasks and accounting for review, rework, defects, and maintenance—not just generation time.I am comfortable delegating more of the work when I can explain what was requested, what changed, and why the evidence supports accepting it. That is the engineering standard I want to carry into AI-assisted development.Which decisions in your workflow remain visible after the conversation ends—and what evidence tells you that the agent respected them?Authorship note: The initial draft was generated with AI assistance from Armando Picón's arguments and a source review. Armando reviewed the article and approved publication. The Spanish translation was produced with AI assistance. The mobile example is hypothetical.

articles.sourceTitle: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
articles.title: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
articles.text:
The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025.
Justin Sullivan | Getty Images

Oracle

filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.

"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.

Stock Chart IconStock chart icon

Oracle's one-day performance

The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.

Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.

Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026

While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.
